comment: Conditional contraindications: combinations that are harmful only when a specific condition / co-medication / lab finding is present. The synergies engine surfaces these alongside the interactions panel — same shape as interactions but with a `condition_required` field.

harms.label: Alcohol + metabolic syndrome / NAFLD
harms.mechanism: Alcohol directly drives hepatic steatosis progression, raises triglycerides, worsens insulin resistance, and elevates ALT. In someone with metabolic syndrome or elevated ALT, even moderate alcohol intake accelerates NAFLD → NASH progression and CV risk.
harms.context: If ALT is elevated or the user has metabolic syndrome, the threshold for 'safe' alcohol is much lower than population guidelines suggest. Consider time-limited abstinence + recheck ALT in 3 months.

harms.label: Calcium + levothyroxine absorption interference
harms.mechanism: Calcium and iron supplements bind levothyroxine in the gut and substantially reduce its absorption. The result: TSH creeps up even on a stable dose. Effect is dose-dependent — high-dose calcium (≥500 mg per dose) is the main offender.
harms.context: Take levothyroxine in the morning fasting; separate from calcium/iron by at least 4 hours.

harms.label: Iron + levothyroxine absorption interference
harms.mechanism: Iron forms an insoluble complex with levothyroxine, reducing T4 absorption by 30-40%. Effect is most pronounced when both are taken simultaneously.
harms.context: Separate iron and levothyroxine by ≥4 hours.

harms.label: High-dose omega-3 + anticoagulation
harms.mechanism: Omega-3s (≥3 g/day EPA+DHA) reduce platelet aggregation and bleeding time. Combined with warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, etc., this raises bleeding risk meaningfully. Recent meta-analyses also flag higher AF risk at very high doses.
harms.context: Clinical practice is to use the lowest effective dose (often 1 g/day) when on anticoagulation, and monitor INR / bleeding signs.

harms.label: Ginkgo + anticoagulation / antiplatelet
harms.mechanism: Ginkgo's PAF antagonism is additive with anticoagulants and antiplatelets. Major bleeding events including intracranial haemorrhage have been reported in case-series.
harms.context: Avoid the combination unless specifically reviewed with the prescribing clinician.

harms.label: Berberine + metformin
harms.mechanism: Berberine has insulin-sensitising effects similar to metformin. Combined use can cause additive hypoglycaemia, especially in lean or older patients with stable glycaemic control.
harms.context: Monitor fasting glucose if adding berberine to metformin; consider reducing metformin dose if A1C trends down.

harms.label: Grapefruit + CYP3A4 substrates
harms.mechanism: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit inhibit intestinal CYP3A4, raising plasma levels of statins (especially simvastatin), some CCBs, and immunosuppressants. The effect persists 24-72h after a single grapefruit dose.
harms.context: Switch to a non-grapefruit-affected statin (rosuvastatin, pravastatin) if grapefruit is important to your diet.

harms.label: Vitamin K + warfarin
harms.mechanism: Vitamin K (K1 from leafy greens, K2 from supplements) directly antagonises warfarin. Sudden changes in K intake — starting a K2 supplement, going leafy-green-heavy or -light — destabilise INR.
harms.context: On warfarin, keep K intake stable rather than starting/stopping supplements. K2 (MK-7) at supplement dose can still meaningfully affect INR.

harms.label: St. John's Wort + multiple drug classes
harms.mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 and P-gp inducer. With SSRIs/SNRIs: serotonin syndrome risk. With oral contraceptives: failure risk (breakthrough pregnancies documented). With warfarin: INR destabilisation. With cyclosporine: organ rejection.
harms.context: Treat as essentially a co-prescription needing pharmacist review.

harms.label: High-dose vitamin C in stone-formers / iron-overload
harms.mechanism: Excess vitamin C is metabolised to oxalate. In stone-formers it raises calcium oxalate stone risk. In haemochromatosis it enhances iron absorption.
harms.context: Keep doses under 500 mg/day in these conditions.

harms.label: SSRI + NSAID / antiplatelet stack
harms.mechanism: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin and impair platelet aggregation. Combined with chronic NSAIDs or antiplatelets, GI bleeding risk roughly doubles vs either alone.
harms.context: If chronic NSAID is required, prefer the SNRI duloxetine which carries less of this effect; consider PPI gastroprotection.

harms.label: K supplementation + RAAS / K-sparing diuretic
harms.mechanism: ACEi/ARB/MRA all raise serum potassium by blocking aldosterone-mediated K excretion. Adding K supplementation can drive serum K into the danger zone (>5.5 mmol/L), risk arrhythmias.
harms.context: Check K before adding any supplement when on these classes.

harms.label: High-dose fish oil + atrial fibrillation
harms.mechanism: REDUCE-IT (icosapent ethyl) showed AF incidence increase at high doses. Recent MAs suggest the effect generalises to high-dose EPA/DHA.
harms.context: If on chronic AF, weigh CV benefit vs AF-recurrence risk with cardiologist.

harms.label: Long-term PPIs in patients with bone fragility
harms.mechanism: Chronic PPI use impairs calcium / magnesium absorption and is associated with fracture risk in observational data. The interaction matters most in patients already at fracture risk.
harms.context: Lowest effective dose + intermittent use where possible; check Mg + 25(OH)D periodically.

harms.label: Creatine + CKD
harms.mechanism: Creatine itself appears safe in most studies of CKD patients, but it raises serum creatinine via non-renal means, confounding eGFR estimation. In advanced CKD where eGFR trends matter clinically, this creates monitoring noise rather than direct harm.
harms.context: If on creatine, mention it to your nephrologist; use cystatin C-based eGFR for monitoring.
